chapters.title: Design for a specific audience
chapters.goal: Land on a print design and audience narrow enough that only that group would truly understand and want it.
explanation: Start from a specific group you're already part of — a hobby, an inside joke, a niche fandom, a specific sport or subculture — generic designs for "everyone" rarely sell.
Browse existing print-on-demand marketplaces for your niche to see what's already selling and what's missing or done badly.
Sketch or mock up 3-5 design concepts before committing to one, and get real feedback from people in the actual target group.

Make sure your idea is 100% original — no fan art, band logos, movie quotes, or sports team names without a license, since this is the single most common reason print-on-demand accounts get shut down.
Write your one-sentence pitch: "For people who [specific interest], this design says [what]."
chapters.example: Tomer was deep into a specific indie board game community. He designed an original illustration referencing an inside joke from that community — not the game's actual logo or art, which would have been a copyright problem — and it immediately made sense to anyone in that community.
mistakes: Designing something generic that could apply to any audience, which rarely stands out enough to sell.
Using copyrighted characters, logos or quotes without a license — the top reason accounts get shut down in this business.
Committing to one design without getting feedback from real people in the target group first.
chapters.template:
Design worksheet:
Specific audience/niche: ____
Existing designs I researched, and what's missing: ____
3-5 concepts sketched — feedback from real target-group members: ____
Originality check: 100% my own work, no copyrighted characters/logos/quotes? Yes/No
One-sentence pitch: "For people who ____, this design says ____."
checklist: Identified a specific, narrow target audience
Researched existing designs in that niche
Sketched multiple concepts and got real feedback
Confirmed the design is 100% original with no copyright risk

chapters.title: Know your buyer's specific taste
chapters.goal: Understand exactly what visual style and message this audience actually buys, not just what they'd casually like.
explanation: There's a difference between an audience liking a design and buying it — look at what similar niches actually purchase (best-sellers on similar print-on-demand stores), not just what gets likes on social media.
Notice the specific visual style this audience responds to (minimalist line art vs. bold color vs. text-based humor) by studying existing successful designs in adjacent niches.
Find where this audience actually is online — a specific subreddit, Discord, or hashtag — and spend time there understanding their inside references and humor.
Write a short profile: who they are, what occasion they'd buy this for (for themselves, as a gift, for an event), and what would make them choose your design specifically.
Show 2-3 finished mockups to real people in this audience and ask directly: "would you actually buy this, and why or why not?"
chapters.example: Tomer's audience profile: "People active in this specific board game community who'd wear the shirt to game nights or conventions as a recognizable in-group signal." That reframed his design toward something instantly recognizable to insiders, not broadly appealing.
mistakes: Confusing social media likes with actual buying intent — very different signals.
Designing in a visual style that doesn't match what this specific audience actually purchases.
Never directly asking real target-audience members if they'd actually buy it.
chapters.template:
Audience one-pager:
Who: ____
Occasion they'd buy for: ____
Visual style that resonates (from research): ____
"Would you buy this?" feedback from 2-3 real people: ____
checklist: Studied best-sellers in adjacent niches, not just liked social posts
Identified the visual style this audience actually buys
Found where this audience spends time online
Asked real target-audience members directly if they'd buy it

chapters.title: Price for the print-on-demand margin
chapters.goal: Set a price that leaves real margin after the platform's printing cost, which is usually higher per-unit than bulk manufacturing.
explanation: Check the print-on-demand platform's base cost for your exact product (shirt style, mug type, poster size/paper) — this varies a lot by product and platform.
A common approach: price = base cost + a fixed margin you're comfortable with, then sanity-check against what similar designs sell for on the same platform.

Remember print-on-demand base costs are higher per unit than bulk manufacturing, so percentage-based multipliers from other business models don't always translate directly — check the actual dollar margin, not just a percentage.
Factor in the platform's own transaction/selling fees (if selling on a marketplace like Etsy or Redbubble) on top of the base print cost.
Decide if you'll offer multiple product types (shirt, mug, poster) at launch or start with just one — one well-priced product beats five half-considered ones.
chapters.example: Tomer's shirt design had a $12.40 base print cost on his platform. He priced at $27.99, leaving about $15.50 before the marketplace's own selling fees, and checked that similar niche designs sold in the $24-32 range.
mistakes: Using a generic multiplier without checking the platform's actual base cost, which varies significantly by product.
Forgetting marketplace selling fees on top of the print cost when calculating real margin.
Launching 8 product types at once instead of nailing the price and demand for one first.
chapters.template:
Pricing calculator:
Platform base print cost: $____
My price: $____
Margin before marketplace fees: $____
Marketplace fee (if applicable): ____% → real margin: $____
Competitor price range for similar niche designs: $____ – $____
checklist: Checked the platform's actual base print cost for the specific product
Set a price with real dollar margin, not just a rough percentage
Accounted for marketplace selling fees
Started with one product type before expanding

chapters.title: Costs and startup budget
chapters.goal: Know that uploading a design is essentially free, and the only real cost is optional advertising.
explanation: Print-on-demand is one of the lowest-risk paths here — you never pay for stock, since items only print after a sale. Uploading designs is typically free.
The main potential cost is design software (many free options exist, like Canva's free tier) and, optionally, paid advertising to reach beyond organic marketplace traffic.
Order one physical sample of your own design before promoting it — checking print quality and color accuracy on the actual platform/product matters, since colors on screen don't always match print.
If testing paid ads, set a small hard cap you're prepared to lose completely, same as any other paid-traffic test in this app.
Track any recurring costs (a paid design tool subscription) and cancel anything unused after a free trial.
chapters.example: Tomer spent $0 to launch — free design software and free platform listing. His only cost was ordering one $14 sample shirt to check the actual print quality before telling anyone about the store.
mistakes: Skipping a physical sample order and discovering a color/quality problem only after a customer complains.
Spending on paid ads before confirming the design and print quality are actually good.
Forgetting a free design-tool trial converts to a paid subscription.
chapters.template:
Startup cost sheet:
Design tool (free/paid): ____
Sample ordered for quality check? Yes/No — cost: $____
Ad test hard cap (if any): $____
checklist: Confirmed uploading and listing designs is free on my chosen platform
Ordered a physical sample to check print quality
Set a hard cap for any ad testing
Checked for any free-trial tools about to convert to paid

chapters.title: Build a recognizable store
chapters.goal: Make your print-on-demand store feel like a curated collection with a point of view, not a random design dump.
explanation: Pick a store name that fits your niche's tone, and check it's not already taken or an obvious trademark conflict.
Keep a consistent visual style across your designs (a recurring color palette, line style, or theme) so the store feels curated rather than random.
Write a store description that speaks directly to your specific audience, referencing the shared interest/community, not a generic "cool designs" tagline.
Use real mockup photos (people or realistic product shots) rather than only flat design previews — it helps buyers imagine actually owning it.
State your policy on requests/customization clearly if you accept them, and just as clearly if you don't, to set expectations.
chapters.example: Tomer's store name directly referenced the board game community's own slang, and every design shared a consistent minimalist line-art style — regulars in the community recognized his shop's "look" within a few designs.
mistakes: A generic store name/description that doesn't signal it's made specifically for this audience.
Wildly inconsistent visual styles across designs, making the store feel random.
Using only flat design previews with no realistic product mockups.
chapters.template:
Store brand basics:
Store name (checked for conflicts): ____
Consistent visual theme: ____
Store description (specific to audience): "____"
Customization policy: ____
checklist: Picked a store name fitting the niche's tone
Kept a consistent visual style across designs
Wrote a specific, audience-aware store description
Used realistic mockups, not just flat previews

chapters.title: Choose where to sell and promote
chapters.goal: Pick the right marketplace and promotion channel to reach a niche audience efficiently.
explanation: Marketplaces with built-in search traffic (like Redbubble or Etsy) can get you discovered without any marketing — worth using alongside or instead of a standalone store, especially early on.
For promotion, go directly to where your specific niche audience already gathers (a subreddit, Discord, community hashtag) rather than broad, generic social posting.
Photograph or film real people wearing/using the product for social content — real-use photos consistently outperform plain product mockups for conversion.
If running paid ads, keep the audience targeting as narrow and specific as the design itself — broad targeting wastes budget on people who'll never recognize the reference.
Track which platform/channel actually drives sales, not just views, and focus effort there.
chapters.example: Tomer listed on Redbubble for built-in search traffic, and separately shared real-use photos (friends wearing the shirt at a game night) directly in the community's own Discord, which converted far better than any broad social post.
mistakes: Only building a standalone store with no existing marketplace traffic to rely on.
Promoting broadly instead of directly in the specific community that would understand the reference.
Running ads with broad targeting for a design that only makes sense to a narrow group.
chapters.template:
Channel plan:
Marketplace(s) used: ____
Primary promotion channel (specific community): ____
Real-use content plan: ____
checklist: Listed on at least one marketplace with built-in traffic
Promoted directly in the specific community the design targets
Created real-use photo/video content, not just flat mockups
Tracked which channel actually drives sales

chapters.title: Land your first sale
chapters.goal: Get one real stranger (or community member) to buy your design.
explanation: Make sure your listing has clear sizing/product info and accurate mockup images before promoting it anywhere.
Share it authentically where your niche audience already trusts you — a real community member sharing something they made often converts better than an obvious ad.
Respond quickly to any questions about sizing, print quality, or shipping time — new-brand buyers are more hesitant and questions are often the last step before buying.
Consider a small launch discount to get your first review, since early social proof matters a lot for a completely new, unproven store.
Log what led to the first sale — which platform, which specific post or share — so you can repeat exactly that.
chapters.example: Tomer's first sale came directly after he shared the design (as a genuine community member, not a marketer) in the game's Discord, offering a small launch discount to the first five buyers as thanks for the community's support.
mistakes: Promoting before the listing has clear, accurate sizing and product information.
Coming across as an outside marketer rather than a genuine member of the community being sold to.
Going silent on pre-purchase questions about sizing or shipping.
chapters.template:
First-sale log:
Listing checked for clear sizing/info before promoting? Yes/No
First sale source: ____
Questions asked before buying: "____"
checklist: Confirmed listing has clear, accurate product information
Shared authentically within the target community
Replied quickly to any pre-purchase questions
Logged the source of the first real sale

chapters.title: Handle sizing, quality and complaints
chapters.goal: Keep buyers happy despite not personally controlling the actual printing and shipping.
explanation: Since the platform handles printing and shipping, your service role is mostly setting accurate expectations upfront and handling issues fast when the platform gets something wrong.
Provide a clear sizing guide (not just "true to size") since apparel sizing varies by brand/platform and is a common source of returns.
Have a clear process ready for print defects or shipping problems — most platforms offer free reprints/refunds for their own errors, so know that policy before a customer asks.
Respond to reviews, especially critical ones, professionally — a print-on-demand platform issue that gets handled well often turns into a positive follow-up review.
Keep a running note of any recurring quality issues with a specific product/platform, and consider switching print providers if problems repeat.
chapters.example: When a customer's shirt arrived with a slightly misprinted design, Tomer immediately used the platform's free-reprint policy for their error, and the customer's follow-up comment specifically praised the fast resolution.
mistakes: Vague "true to size" sizing info instead of a real, specific size guide.
Not knowing the platform's own defect/reprint policy before a customer complains.
Ignoring recurring quality issues instead of considering a provider switch.
chapters.template:
Service playbook:
Sizing guide provided? Yes/No
Platform's defect/reprint policy: ____
Recurring quality issues noted: ____
checklist: Provided a specific, real sizing guide
Knew the platform's defect/reprint policy before it was needed
Responded professionally to at least one review
Tracked any recurring quality issues

chapters.title: Payments and payouts
chapters.goal: Get paid legally through the print-on-demand platform's payout system.
explanation: Most print-on-demand marketplaces and payout systems require an 18+ account holder — under that age, a parent opens and holds the account.
Understand the platform's payout schedule and minimum threshold before expecting a specific payout date.
Agree the transfer arrangement with the account-holding parent before sales start generating real payouts.
Keep your own simple log of sales and payouts, separate from the platform's dashboard, since access to that dashboard could change.
Never share account login details or one-time codes with anyone outside your agreed arrangement.
chapters.example: Tomer's Redbubble and Etsy accounts were both registered under his father's details, with payouts transferring to Tomer's own account monthly after the platform's own payout schedule cleared.
mistakes: Registering accounts without meeting the platform's age requirement, risking account or payout issues later.
Not knowing the payout threshold/schedule and being confused when money doesn't arrive as expected.
Sharing account access outside the agreed family arrangement.
chapters.template:
Payment setup record:
Platform account holder (18+): ____
Payout schedule and minimum threshold: ____
Agreed transfer arrangement to me: ____
checklist: Confirmed the account holder meets the platform's age requirement
Understood the payout schedule and minimum threshold
Agreed the transfer arrangement with the account-holding parent
Kept my own separate sales/payout log
chapters.parentNote: Print-on-demand marketplaces and their payout systems generally require an 18+ account holder. A parent needs to hold this account under this age.

chapters.title: Accounting and taxes
chapters.goal: Track design-by-design profit and understand what's owed.
explanation: Print-on-demand income is taxable business income in almost every country, including for minors, with specifics that vary by country.
Keep a log per sale: design, sale price, platform's base print cost, platform selling fee, and net profit — this also tells you which designs are actually worth making more of.
Set aside a percentage of net profit (a rough 20-25% placeholder is common) rather than spending all payouts immediately.
Watch for platforms that issue a tax form once you cross an earnings threshold, and keep your own records either way.
Have one real conversation with a parent, and once income is more than pocket change, check your country's actual rules for minors' business income.
chapters.example: Tomer's spreadsheet tracked net profit per design, which also revealed his second design was actually more profitable per sale than his first, despite selling fewer units.
mistakes: Tracking gross sales instead of net profit after print cost and platform fees.
Not tracking profit per design, missing which specific designs are actually worth expanding.
Spending all payouts immediately with nothing set aside.
chapters.template:
Design profit log (one row per design):
Design | Units sold | Sale price | Print cost | Platform fee | Net profit
Monthly set-aside: ____% = $____
checklist: Started a running log tracking net profit per design
Set aside a percentage of net profit
Checked whether the platform issues a tax form
Had one conversation with a parent about this income
chapters.parentNote: Print-on-demand income is taxable in most places, including for minors, and this needs a parent involved plus a real check with local tax rules once income is meaningful.

chapters.title: Growing your design catalog
chapters.goal: Turn one working design into a small, growing catalog of proven sellers.
explanation: Look at which design and which specific product type (shirt vs. mug vs. poster) actually sold, and make more variations in that proven direction before branching into unrelated designs.
Expand into adjacent niches or related inside references within the same broad community, reusing what you've already learned about their taste.
Retire designs that aren't selling after a fair test period, rather than letting an overcrowded store dilute attention from your proven winners.
Consider a small paid ad test only once you have at least one proven, consistently-selling design to promote.
Review monthly: which designs sold, real profit per design, and what the data suggests trying next — not daily view counts.
chapters.example: After his first design sold steadily for two months, Tomer made three variations referencing other inside jokes from the same community, using the same proven visual style — two of the three became solid additional sellers.
mistakes: Branching into unrelated niches before proving the first design's audience and style actually converts.
Letting an overcrowded, unfocused catalog of untested designs dilute attention from proven sellers.
Running paid ads before having any proven-selling design to promote.
chapters.template:
Monthly growth review:
Best-selling design(s) and product type: ____
Net profit this month: $____
Next design variation planned, based on proven style: ____
checklist: Identified which design/product type actually sold
Made new designs building on the proven style, not unrelated ones
Retired designs that weren't selling after a fair test
Set up a monthly review of sales and profit by design
